In [[numerical methods]] for [[stochastic differential equations]], the '''Markov chain approximation method (MCAM)''' belongs to the several numerical (schemes) approaches used in [[stochastic control theory]]. Regrettably the simple adaptation of the deterministic schemes for matching up to stochastic models such as the Runge–Kutta method does not work at all.

It is a powerful and widely usable set of ideas, due to the current infancy of stochastic control it might be even said 'insights.' for numerical and other approximations problems in [[stochastic processes]].<ref>Harold J Kushner, Paul G Dupuis, Numerical methods for stochastic control problems in continuous time, Applications of mathematics 24, Springer-Verlag, 1992.</ref><ref>[[Peter Kloeden|P E Kloeden]], [[Eckhard Platen]], Numerical Solutions of Stochastic Differential Equations, Applications of Mathematics  23, Stochastic Modelling and Applied probability, Springer, 1992.</ref> They represent counterparts from deterministic control theory such as [[optimal control theory]].<ref>F. B. Hanson, [http://homepages.math.uic.edu/~hanson/pub/CADS96/cads96mca.pdf "Markov Chain Approximation"], in C. T. Leondes, ed., ''Stochastic Digital Control System Techniques'', Academic Press, 1996, {{isbn|978-0120127764}}.</ref>

The basic idea of the MCAM is to approximate the original [[controlled process]] by a chosen [[controlled markov process]] on a [[finite state space]]. In case of need, one must as well approximate the [[cost function (control theory)|cost function]] for one that matches up the [[Markov chain]] chosen to approximate the original stochastic process.
